CHAPTER 19 - CLASSIFICATION OF LIVING ORGANISMS

Introduction

Our planet is home to an enormous diversity of living organisms - from microscopic bacteria to giant whales, from tiny mosses to towering trees. Scientists have so far described well over a million species, and many more remain unknown. To study, name, compare and communicate about such a vast number of organisms, biologists arrange them into orderly groups. This arrangement of organisms into groups and sub-groups on the basis of their similarities and differences is called CLASSIFICATION. The branch of biology that deals with classification, identification and naming of organisms is called TAXONOMY (or systematics).

19.1 NEED AND ADVANTAGES OF CLASSIFICATION

Imagine a library with millions of books but no shelves, no catalogue and no order - finding a single book would be almost impossible. Living organisms present a similar challenge. Classification solves it. Its advantages are:
 - It makes the study of a huge variety of organisms simple and systematic; instead of studying each organism separately, we study representative members of each group.
 - It shows the relationships among different groups of organisms and reveals how they may have evolved from common ancestors.
 - It helps in the correct identification and naming of organisms, avoiding confusion caused by local names.
 - It provides a worldwide common scientific language, so a scientist in India and one in Japan refer to the same organism by the same name.
 - It forms the basis for other branches of biology such as ecology, evolution and biogeography.

19.2 BASIS OF CLASSIFICATION

Organisms are grouped using several characteristics. The most important bases are:
 (a) CELL TYPE - whether the cell is PROKARYOTIC (no true membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, e.g. bacteria) or EUKARYOTIC (a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, e.g. plants, animals, fungi, protists). This is the most fundamental division of life.
 (b) CELL NUMBER - whether the organism is UNICELLULAR (a single cell carries out all functions, e.g. Amoeba, bacteria) or MULTICELLULAR (made of many cells with division of labour, e.g. mango tree, human).
 (c) MODE OF NUTRITION - whether the organism is AUTOTROPHIC (prepares its own food by photosynthesis, e.g. green plants) or HETEROTROPHIC (depends on others for food, e.g. animals, fungi).
 (d) BODY ORGANISATION - the level of complexity of the body, from simple cellular grade to tissue, organ and organ-system grades; and features such as the presence of a true coelom (body cavity), symmetry and segmentation.

19.3 THE TWO-KINGDOM SYSTEM AND ITS LIMITATIONS

For a long time, following Carolus Linnaeus, all living things were placed in just TWO KINGDOMS - PLANTAE (plants) and ANIMALIA (animals). Organisms that were green, fixed and made their own food were plants; those that moved and ate food were animals. This simple scheme had serious LIMITATIONS:
 - It did not separate prokaryotes (bacteria) from eukaryotes, although their cells are fundamentally different.
 - It grouped unicellular and multicellular organisms together.
 - Organisms such as fungi (which do not photosynthesise) were wrongly placed with plants.
 - Euglena, which both moves like an animal and photosynthesises like a plant, could not be placed satisfactorily in either kingdom.
These problems showed the need for a better, more natural system.

19.4 WHITTAKER'S FIVE KINGDOM CLASSIFICATION

In 1969, R. H. Whittaker proposed the FIVE KINGDOM classification, which is widely used today. He used three main criteria: cell structure (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular/multicellular) and mode of nutrition. The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

(1) KINGDOM MONERA: Prokaryotic organisms - they have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. They are unicellular. Some have a cell wall. Nutrition is either autotrophic or heterotrophic. Examples: bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), mycoplasma. They are the simplest and most ancient organisms.

(2) KINGDOM PROTISTA: Unicellular EUKARYOTES with a true nucleus. They may have locomotory structures such as cilia or flagella. Nutrition is autotrophic or heterotrophic. They form a link between Monera and the higher kingdoms. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena, diatoms.

(3) KINGDOM FUNGI: Eukaryotic, mostly multicellular (yeast is unicellular). Their cell walls are made of CHITIN. They are HETEROTROPHIC and SAPROPHYTIC - they obtain food by absorbing nutrients from dead and decaying matter; some are parasites. They store food as glycogen. Examples: mushrooms, Rhizopus (bread mould), yeast, Penicillium. Some fungi live in symbiotic association with algae as LICHENS.

(4) KINGDOM PLANTAE: Eukaryotic, multicellular organisms with cell walls made of CELLULOSE. They contain chlorophyll and are AUTOTROPHIC (photosynthetic). Examples: all green plants - algae, mosses, ferns and seed plants.

(5) KINGDOM ANIMALIA: Eukaryotic, multicellular organisms WITHOUT cell walls and without chlorophyll. They are HETEROTROPHIC (holozoic) and most can move about. Examples: all animals - from sponges and worms to insects, fish, birds and mammals.

19.5 HIERARCHY OF CLASSIFICATION

Within each kingdom, organisms are arranged in a series of ranks (taxa), each smaller and more closely related than the one above it. From the largest to the smallest, the hierarchy is:
   KINGDOM > PHYLUM (in animals) or DIVISION (in plants) > CLASS > ORDER > FAMILY > GENUS > SPECIES
As we move down this ladder, the number of organisms in each group DECREASES while the number of shared characteristics INCREASES. The SPECIES is the basic unit of classification - a group of organisms so similar that they can interbreed among themselves and produce fertile offspring. For example, human beings belong to: Kingdom Animalia > Phylum Chordata > Class Mammalia > Order Primata > Family Hominidae > Genus Homo > Species sapiens.

19.6 BINOMIAL NOMENCLATURE

Common names of organisms vary from place to place and language to language, causing confusion. To give every organism a single, universally accepted scientific name, Carolus (Carl) LINNAEUS introduced the system of BINOMIAL NOMENCLATURE. 'Binomial' means 'two names': each organism is given a two-part Latin name. The FIRST part is the GENUS (generic name) and the SECOND part is the SPECIES (specific name). The rules of naming are:
 - The name is written in Latin (or latinised) and is usually printed in ITALICS.
 - When handwritten, both parts are UNDERLINED separately.
 - The genus name BEGINS WITH A CAPITAL letter; the species name begins with a SMALL letter.
Examples: human - Homo sapiens; mango - Mangifera indica; pea - Pisum sativum; common frog - Rana tigrina; house cat - Felis domestica.

19.7 MAJOR GROUPS OF PLANTS

Kingdom Plantae is divided into groups based on the presence of a well-developed body, conducting (vascular) tissue, and seeds:
 (a) THALLOPHYTA (ALGAE): Simple plants with no true roots, stems or leaves; the body is a thallus. Mostly aquatic. Examples: Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Chara.
 (b) BRYOPHYTA: The 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'. They have a simple body differentiated into stem-like and leaf-like parts but NO true vascular tissue; they need water for reproduction. Examples: mosses (Funaria), Marchantia.
 (c) PTERIDOPHYTA: The first plants with true VASCULAR tissue (xylem and phloem) and true roots, stems and leaves, but they bear NO seeds; they reproduce by spores. Examples: ferns (Dryopteris), Marsilea, horsetails.
 (d) GYMNOSPERMS: Seed-bearing plants whose seeds are NAKED (not enclosed in a fruit). They are usually evergreen. Examples: Pinus, Cycas, Cedrus.
 (e) ANGIOSPERMS (flowering plants): Seed-bearing plants whose seeds are enclosed within a FRUIT. They bear flowers. They are divided into two groups: MONOCOTYLEDONS (seed has one cotyledon; parallel leaf venation; fibrous roots; e.g. maize, wheat, grass) and DICOTYLEDONS (seed has two cotyledons; reticulate leaf venation; tap root; e.g. gram, mango, rose).

19.8 MAJOR ANIMAL PHYLA (IN BRIEF)

Kingdom Animalia is divided into many phyla, arranged here roughly in order of increasing complexity:
 - PORIFERA: Pore-bearing animals - the sponges; cellular grade, with a porous body and canal system. e.g. Sycon, Spongilla.
 - COELENTERATA (CNIDARIA): Aquatic animals with a hollow body cavity and stinging cells; radial symmetry. e.g. Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemone.
 - PLATYHELMINTHES: Flatworms; dorsoventrally flattened, bilaterally symmetrical, often parasitic. e.g. Planaria, liver fluke, tapeworm.
 - NEMATODA (Aschelminthes): Roundworms; cylindrical, many parasitic. e.g. Ascaris, filarial worm.
 - ANNELIDA: Segmented worms with a true body cavity (coelom). e.g. earthworm, leech, Nereis.
 - ARTHROPODA: The largest phylum; jointed legs, an exoskeleton of chitin and a segmented body. e.g. insects, prawns, spiders, scorpions.
 - MOLLUSCA: Soft-bodied animals, usually with a hard shell. e.g. snail, octopus, mussel.
 - ECHINODERMATA: Spiny-skinned marine animals with radial symmetry in the adult. e.g. starfish, sea urchin.
 - CHORDATA: Animals with a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord and gill slits at some stage. The advanced chordates (vertebrates) have a backbone. Vertebrates are grouped into FIVE classes: PISCES (fishes - aquatic, gills, scales, fins; e.g. Labeo, shark), AMPHIBIA (live on land and in water, moist skin; e.g. frog, toad), REPTILIA (creeping animals with dry scaly skin; e.g. lizard, snake, turtle), AVES (birds - feathers, wings, beak, warm-blooded; e.g. pigeon, crow), and MAMMALIA (hair on body, mammary glands to feed young, warm-blooded; e.g. human, dog, whale).

SUMMARY

 - Classification is the arrangement of organisms into groups based on similarities and differences; taxonomy is the science of classification, identification and naming.
 - Classification makes study systematic, shows evolutionary relationships and gives a common scientific language.
 - The main bases of classification are cell type (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), cell number (unicellular/multicellular), mode of nutrition (autotrophic/heterotrophic) and body organisation.
 - The old two-kingdom system (Plantae and Animalia) failed to separate prokaryotes, unicellular forms and fungi.
 - Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
 - The classification hierarchy is Kingdom > Phylum/Division > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species; species is the basic unit.
 - Linnaeus's binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part italicised Latin name (capitalised genus + small-letter species), e.g. Homo sapiens, Mangifera indica.
 - Plants are grouped into Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms (monocots and dicots).
 - Animals are grouped into phyla such as Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Chordata (whose vertebrates include Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia).

topics.name: Need and Basis of Classification
topics.description: Why we classify organisms and the advantages of doing so; the main bases of classification - cell type (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), cell number (unicellular/multicellular), mode of nutrition (autotroph/heterotroph) and body organisation; the two-kingdom system and its limitations.

topics.name: Five Kingdom Classification
topics.description: Whittaker's five kingdom system (1969) - Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia - the criteria used and the defining characteristics and examples of each kingdom.

topics.name: Hierarchy of Classification
topics.description: The taxonomic ranks from Kingdom through Phylum/Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus down to Species; how shared characters increase and group size decreases down the ladder; species as the basic unit.

topics.name: Binomial Nomenclature
topics.description: Linnaeus's two-name scientific naming system; the rules of writing scientific names (Latin, italics, capital genus, small-letter species) with examples such as Homo sapiens and Mangifera indica.

topics.name: Classification of Plants
topics.description: Major plant groups - Thallophyta (algae), Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms - and the distinction between monocotyledons and dicotyledons.

topics.name: Classification of Animals
topics.description: Major animal phyla in brief - Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Chordata, including the five vertebrate classes.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain the need for classification of living organisms and state its main advantages.
Describe the main bases of classification (cell type, cell number, mode of nutrition, body organisation) and explain the limitations of the two-kingdom system.
Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker's classification and state the defining characteristics and examples of each.
Compare the five kingdoms using cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition, and classify a given organism into the correct kingdom.
Arrange the taxonomic categories in correct sequence and explain how shared characteristics and group size change down the hierarchy.
State the rules of binomial nomenclature and write/identify scientific names correctly, recognising Linnaeus as its founder.
Distinguish the major plant groups (Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms, Angiosperms) and differentiate monocots from dicots.
Identify the major animal phyla and the five vertebrate classes from their defining characteristics and examples.

chapter_summary.title: Classification of Living Organisms - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 19. It explains why and how living organisms are classified, Whittaker's five kingdom system, the taxonomic hierarchy, binomial nomenclature, and the major groups of plants and animals.

sections.heading: Need and basis of classification
bullets: Classification is the arrangement of organisms into groups and sub-groups based on their similarities and differences; the science of doing this is taxonomy.
It makes the study of millions of organisms simple and systematic, reveals evolutionary relationships, allows correct identification and provides a common scientific language.
Organisms are grouped on the basis of cell type (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), cell number (unicellular or multicellular), mode of nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic) and body organisation.
The old two-kingdom system (Plantae and Animalia) failed because it did not separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes, mixed unicellular with multicellular forms, and wrongly placed fungi with plants.

sections.heading: Whittaker's five kingdom classification
bullets: Proposed by R. H. Whittaker in 1969 using cell structure, body organisation and mode of nutrition.
Monera: prokaryotic, unicellular organisms with no true nucleus (bacteria, blue-green algae). Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena).
Fungi: eukaryotic, mostly multicellular, heterotrophic and saprophytic, with chitin cell walls (mushrooms, yeast, Rhizopus).
Plantae: eukaryotic, multicellular, autotrophic, cellulose cell walls (green plants). Animalia: eukaryotic, multicellular, heterotrophic, no cell wall (all animals).

sections.heading: Hierarchy of classification
bullets: The taxonomic ranks, from largest to smallest, are Kingdom > Phylum (Division in plants) > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species.
Moving down the hierarchy, the number of organisms in a group decreases while the number of shared characteristics increases.
Species is the basic unit of classification - organisms similar enough to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
Example: human - Animalia > Chordata > Mammalia > Primata > Hominidae > Homo > sapiens.

sections.heading: Binomial nomenclature
bullets: Introduced by Carl (Carolus) Linnaeus to give every organism a single, universally accepted scientific name.
Each name has two parts: the genus (generic) name first and the species (specific) name second.
The name is written in Latin and italics; the genus begins with a capital letter and the species with a small letter; when handwritten each part is underlined.
Examples: Homo sapiens (human), Mangifera indica (mango), Pisum sativum (pea).

sections.heading: Major groups of plants and animals
bullets: Plants: Thallophyta (algae), Bryophyta (mosses), Pteridophyta (ferns), Gymnosperms (naked seeds) and Angiosperms (flowering, seeds in a fruit).
Angiosperms are monocots (one cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots) or dicots (two cotyledons, reticulate venation, tap roots).
Animal phyla include Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda (largest), Mollusca, Echinodermata and Chordata.
Vertebrate chordates fall into five classes: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia.

key_takeaways: Classification arranges organisms into groups by similarities and differences, making their study systematic and revealing relationships.
The main bases of classification are cell type, cell number, mode of nutrition and body organisation.
Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
The hierarchy runs Kingdom > Phylum/Division > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species, with species as the basic unit.
Binomial nomenclature, given by Linnaeus, names each organism with an italicised two-part Latin name (capital genus + small species), e.g. Homo sapiens.
Plants are grouped from Thallophyta to Angiosperms (monocots and dicots).
Animals range from Porifera to Chordata, whose vertebrates form five classes (Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia).

glossary.definition: The arrangement of living organisms into groups and sub-groups on the basis of their similarities and differences.
The branch of biology dealing with the classification, identification and naming of living organisms.
An organism whose cells have no true membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, e.g. bacteria.
An organism whose cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, e.g. plants, animals, fungi, protists.
An organism that prepares its own food, usually by photosynthesis, e.g. green plants.
An organism that depends on other organisms for its food, e.g. animals and fungi.
The kingdom of prokaryotic, unicellular organisms such as bacteria and blue-green algae.
The kingdom of unicellular eukaryotic organisms such as Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena.
The kingdom of eukaryotic, mostly multicellular, saprophytic organisms with chitin cell walls, e.g. mushrooms and yeast.
The basic unit of classification; a group of similar organisms able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
The system, given by Linnaeus, of naming each organism with two Latin words: the genus and the species.
Simple plants (algae) with no true roots, stems or leaves; the body is a thallus, e.g. Spirogyra.
Seedless vascular plants with true roots, stems and leaves that reproduce by spores, e.g. ferns.
A flowering plant whose seeds are enclosed within a fruit; includes monocots and dicots.
The animal phylum whose members have a notochord, dorsal nerve cord and gill slits; vertebrates have a backbone.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Classification of Living Organisms (NIOS)
worksheet.instructions: This is a NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 19. Attempt all questions. Write scientific names in the correct format.

questions.question: What is classification? State any three advantages of classifying living organisms.
questions.answer: Classification is the arrangement of living organisms into groups and sub-groups on the basis of their similarities and differences. Three advantages: (1) it makes the study of a huge variety of organisms simple and systematic, as we study representative members of each group; (2) it shows the relationships among groups and how they may have evolved from common ancestors; (3) it provides a common scientific language and helps in the correct identification and naming of organisms worldwide.
questions.explanation: Definition plus any three valid advantages.

questions.question: List the four main bases on which living organisms are classified.
questions.answer: (1) Cell type - prokaryotic (no true nucleus, e.g. bacteria) or eukaryotic (true nucleus, e.g. plants and animals). (2) Cell number - unicellular (single cell, e.g. Amoeba) or multicellular (many cells, e.g. mango tree). (3) Mode of nutrition - autotrophic (makes its own food, e.g. green plants) or heterotrophic (depends on others, e.g. animals, fungi). (4) Body organisation - level of body complexity such as cellular, tissue, organ and organ-system grades, and features like symmetry and body cavity.
questions.explanation: Cell type, cell number, mode of nutrition and body organisation.

questions.question: Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker's classification and give one defining feature and one example of each.
questions.answer: (1) Monera - prokaryotic, unicellular organisms with no true nucleus; example: bacteria (or blue-green algae). (2) Protista - unicellular eukaryotes with a true nucleus; example: Amoeba (or Paramecium, Euglena). (3) Fungi - eukaryotic, heterotrophic/saprophytic organisms with chitin cell walls; example: mushroom (or yeast, Rhizopus). (4) Plantae - eukaryotic, multicellular, autotrophic organisms with cellulose cell walls; example: mango tree (any green plant). (5) Animalia - eukaryotic, multicellular, heterotrophic organisms with no cell wall; example: human (any animal).
questions.explanation: Whittaker (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia with one feature and example each.

questions.question: Write the taxonomic hierarchy from the largest category to the smallest.
questions.answer: Kingdom > Phylum (Division in plants) > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species. As we move down this hierarchy, the number of organisms in a group decreases while the number of shared characteristics increases. Species is the smallest and basic unit of classification.
questions.explanation: Correct sequence of the seven major taxa.

questions.question: State any three rules of binomial nomenclature and give one example of a scientific name.
questions.answer: Rules: (1) the name has two parts - the genus (first) and the species (second); (2) it is written in Latin and printed in italics (underlined separately when handwritten); (3) the genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter. Example: Homo sapiens (human) or Mangifera indica (mango).
questions.explanation: Any three rules plus a correctly written example.

questions.question: Differentiate between monocotyledons and dicotyledons (any three points).
questions.answer: Monocots: (1) seed has one cotyledon; (2) leaves show parallel venation; (3) fibrous root system; examples - maize, wheat, grass. Dicots: (1) seed has two cotyledons; (2) leaves show reticulate (net-like) venation; (3) tap root system; examples - gram, mango, rose.
questions.explanation: Number of cotyledons, venation and root system distinguish them.

questions.question: Describe the main characteristics of Kingdom Fungi and explain why fungi were wrongly placed with plants in the old two-kingdom system.
questions.answer: Characteristics of Fungi: they are eukaryotic; mostly multicellular (yeast is unicellular); their cell walls are made of chitin; they are heterotrophic and mainly saprophytic, absorbing nutrients from dead and decaying matter (some are parasites); they store food as glycogen. Examples: mushrooms, Rhizopus, yeast, Penicillium. In the old two-kingdom system, fungi were placed with plants because, like plants, they are non-motile (fixed in one place) and possess a cell wall. However, fungi do NOT contain chlorophyll and cannot make their own food, so they are not autotrophic like plants - which is why a separate kingdom was needed for them.
questions.explanation: Features of Fungi plus the reason (non-motile, cell wall) for the historical misplacement, and the correction (no chlorophyll, heterotrophic).

questions.question: Name the five classes of vertebrates and give one example of each.
questions.answer: (1) Pisces (fishes) - e.g. Labeo / shark; (2) Amphibia - e.g. frog / toad; (3) Reptilia - e.g. lizard / snake; (4) Aves (birds) - e.g. pigeon / crow; (5) Mammalia - e.g. human / dog. All belong to phylum Chordata and possess a backbone.
questions.explanation: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia with examples.

questions.question: Why was the two-kingdom system of classification replaced? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: The two-kingdom system (Plantae and Animalia) was replaced because: (1) it did not separate prokaryotes (bacteria) from eukaryotes even though their cells are fundamentally different, and it mixed unicellular forms with multicellular ones; (2) it could not satisfactorily place organisms such as fungi (non-photosynthetic, yet placed with plants) and Euglena (which both moves like an animal and photosynthesises like a plant). A more natural system - Whittaker's five kingdoms - was therefore adopted.
questions.explanation: Failure to separate prokaryotes/eukaryotes and unicellular/multicellular; problem organisms like fungi and Euglena.

questions.question: Classify the following into the correct kingdom: (a) Amoeba (b) mushroom (c) bacterium (d) mango tree.
questions.answer: (a) Amoeba - Protista (unicellular eukaryote). (b) Mushroom - Fungi (heterotrophic, chitin cell wall). (c) Bacterium - Monera (prokaryotic, unicellular, no true nucleus). (d) Mango tree - Plantae (multicellular, autotrophic, cellulose cell wall).
questions.explanation: Apply the defining features of each kingdom to place each organism.

Birds belong to the class
Frogs, which live both on land and in water with moist skin, belong to
questions.explanation: Amphibians live in water and on land.

questions.question: Mammals are distinguished from other vertebrates by the presence of
questions.explanation: Mammary glands and hair are mammalian features.

questions.question: A vertebrate with dry scaly skin that creeps on land is a
Taxonomy is the branch of biology that deals with the classification and naming of organisms.
Bacteria are eukaryotic organisms.
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotic - they have no true nucleus.

questions.question: The two-kingdom system successfully separated prokaryotes from eukaryotes.
questions.explanation: It failed to separate them; this was a major limitation.

questions.question: The five kingdom classification was given by R. H. Whittaker.
Fungi are autotrophic organisms.
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophic/saprophytic; they cannot make their own food.

questions.question: The cell wall of fungi is made of cellulose.
questions.explanation: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose.

questions.question: Species is the basic unit of classification.
questions.explanation: Species is the smallest and basic taxon.

questions.question: In a scientific name the genus name begins with a capital letter.
questions.explanation: Genus is capitalised; species is lowercase.

questions.question: Gymnosperms bear seeds enclosed within a fruit.
questions.explanation: Gymnosperm seeds are naked; angiosperm seeds are enclosed in a fruit.

questions.question: Arthropoda is the largest phylum in the animal kingdom.
questions.explanation: It includes insects, crustaceans, spiders, etc.

questions.question: The science of classification, identification and naming of organisms is called ____.
Organisms that prepare their own food are called ____.
A cell with a true membrane-bound nucleus is said to be ____.
The five kingdom classification was proposed by ____.
The kingdom that contains prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria is ____.
The cell wall of fungi is made of ____.
questions.explanation: Chitin, unlike the cellulose of plants.

questions.question: Unicellular eukaryotes such as Amoeba are placed in the kingdom ____.
The basic unit of classification is the ____.
In plants, the rank equivalent to the animal 'Phylum' is the ____.
The two-name naming system of organisms is called ____.
The scientific name of human beings is ____.
Plants that bear naked seeds are called ____.
A seed having two cotyledons belongs to a ____.
Animals having a notochord and dorsal nerve cord belong to the phylum ____.
Birds belong to the vertebrate class ____.
Define classification and taxonomy.
questions.answer: Classification is the arrangement of living organisms into groups and sub-groups on the basis of their similarities and differences. Taxonomy is the branch of biology that deals with the classification, identification and naming of organisms.

questions.question: Give three advantages of classifying living organisms.
questions.answer: (1) It makes the study of the huge variety of organisms simple and systematic, as representative members of each group are studied. (2) It reveals the relationships among different groups and how they may have evolved. (3) It provides a common scientific language and helps in correct identification and naming worldwide.

questions.question: Distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
questions.answer: A prokaryotic cell has NO true membrane-bound nucleus and lacks membrane-bound organelles; its genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm (e.g. bacteria). A eukaryotic cell has a TRUE nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane and contains membrane-bound organelles (e.g. cells of plants, animals, fungi and protists).
questions.explanation: Presence/absence of true nucleus and organelles.

questions.question: Differentiate between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition with one example each.
questions.answer: Autotrophic nutrition: the organism prepares its own food, usually by photosynthesis - e.g. green plants. Heterotrophic nutrition: the organism depends on other organisms for food - e.g. animals (or fungi).

questions.question: State three limitations of the two-kingdom system of classification.
questions.answer: (1) It did not separate prokaryotes (bacteria) from eukaryotes although their cells are fundamentally different. (2) It grouped unicellular and multicellular organisms together. (3) It wrongly placed non-photosynthetic fungi with plants, and organisms like Euglena (animal-like movement plus plant-like photosynthesis) could not be placed satisfactorily.

questions.question: Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker's classification.
questions.answer: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.question: Write three characteristics of Kingdom Monera with one example.
questions.answer: (1) Members are prokaryotic - they have no true membrane-bound nucleus. (2) They are unicellular. (3) Some have a cell wall; nutrition may be autotrophic or heterotrophic. Example: bacteria (or blue-green algae / cyanobacteria).

questions.question: List three characteristics of Kingdom Fungi.
questions.answer: (1) They are eukaryotic and mostly multicellular (yeast is unicellular). (2) Their cell walls are made of chitin. (3) They are heterotrophic and mainly saprophytic, absorbing nutrients from dead and decaying matter; they store food as glycogen. Examples: mushrooms, Rhizopus, yeast.

questions.question: How does Kingdom Plantae differ from Kingdom Animalia?
questions.answer: Plantae: eukaryotic, multicellular organisms with cellulose cell walls, contain chlorophyll and are autotrophic (make their own food); usually non-motile. Animalia: eukaryotic, multicellular organisms without cell walls and without chlorophyll, heterotrophic, and most can move about.
questions.explanation: Cell wall, chlorophyll, nutrition and movement.

questions.question: On what three criteria did Whittaker base his five kingdom classification?
questions.answer: Whittaker used: (1) cell structure - whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic; (2) body organisation - whether the organism is unicellular or multicellular; and (3) mode of nutrition - whether it is autotrophic or heterotrophic (and the type of heterotrophy, e.g. absorptive in fungi versus ingestive in animals).
questions.explanation: The three criteria of the five kingdom system.

questions.question: Why were fungi given a kingdom separate from plants?
questions.answer: In the old system fungi were placed with plants because, like plants, they are non-motile and have a cell wall. However, fungi do not contain chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise; they are heterotrophic (saprophytic), absorbing food from dead matter, and their cell walls are made of chitin (not cellulose). These fundamental differences in nutrition and cell-wall composition justified placing them in a separate Kingdom Fungi.

questions.question: Classify the following into their kingdoms: bacterium, Paramecium, mushroom, dog.
questions.answer: Bacterium - Monera (prokaryotic, unicellular). Paramecium - Protista (unicellular eukaryote). Mushroom - Fungi (heterotrophic, chitin wall). Dog - Animalia (multicellular, heterotrophic, no cell wall).
questions.explanation: Apply defining features of each kingdom.

questions.question: Write the taxonomic hierarchy from Kingdom to Species.
questions.answer: Kingdom > Phylum (Division in plants) > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species.
questions.explanation: Correct order of the seven major taxa.

questions.question: How do the number of organisms and the number of shared characteristics change as we move down the classification hierarchy?
questions.answer: As we move down the hierarchy (from Kingdom towards Species), the number of organisms included in each group DECREASES, because the groups become more specific. At the same time, the number of characteristics shared by the members INCREASES, because organisms in lower groups are more closely related and more similar to one another.
questions.explanation: Fewer organisms, more shared characters going down.

questions.question: Write the complete classification of human beings from Kingdom to Species.
questions.answer: Kingdom - Animalia; Phylum - Chordata; Class - Mammalia; Order - Primata; Family - Hominidae; Genus - Homo; Species - sapiens. Thus the scientific name of human beings is Homo sapiens.

questions.question: Who introduced binomial nomenclature, and what does 'binomial' mean?
questions.answer: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by Carl (Carolus) Linnaeus. 'Binomial' means a name consisting of two parts (two words): the genus name and the species name.

questions.question: State the rules for writing a scientific name.
questions.answer: (1) The name has two parts: the genus (generic) name first and the species (specific) name second. (2) It is written in Latin (or latinised) words and printed in italics; when handwritten, each part is underlined separately. (3) The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a small (lowercase) letter. Example: Homo sapiens.

questions.question: Write the scientific names of mango and pea, naming the genus in each.
questions.answer: Mango: Mangifera indica - genus Mangifera, species indica. Pea: Pisum sativum - genus Pisum, species sativum. Both should be written in italics with the genus capitalised.

questions.question: Name the five major groups of plants.
questions.answer: Thallophyta (algae), Bryophyta (mosses), Pteridophyta (ferns), Gymnosperms (naked-seeded plants) and Angiosperms (flowering plants).
questions.explanation: The five plant groups in order of complexity.

questions.question: Differentiate between Bryophyta and Pteridophyta.
questions.answer: Bryophyta (e.g. mosses): the body is differentiated into stem-like and leaf-like parts but has NO true vascular (conducting) tissue; they need water for reproduction and are called 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'. Pteridophyta (e.g. ferns): they have true roots, stems and leaves and well-developed vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), but they bear NO seeds and reproduce by spores.
questions.explanation: Vascular tissue and true organs distinguish them.

questions.question: Differentiate between gymnosperms and angiosperms.
questions.answer: Gymnosperms bear NAKED seeds that are not enclosed in a fruit; they usually do not bear true flowers and are often evergreen (e.g. Pinus, Cycas). Angiosperms are flowering plants whose seeds are ENCLOSED within a fruit; they bear flowers and include both monocots and dicots (e.g. mango, wheat).
questions.explanation: Naked seeds vs seeds enclosed in a fruit.

questions.question: Give three differences between monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants.
questions.answer: Monocots: (1) seed has ONE cotyledon; (2) leaves show PARALLEL venation; (3) fibrous root system (e.g. maize, wheat). Dicots: (1) seed has TWO cotyledons; (2) leaves show RETICULATE (net-like) venation; (3) tap root system (e.g. gram, mango).
questions.explanation: Cotyledon number, venation and root system.

questions.question: Name the five classes of vertebrates.
questions.answer: Pisces (fishes), Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves (birds) and Mammalia.

questions.question: Give the defining feature and one example each for Porifera, Coelenterata and Arthropoda.
questions.answer: Porifera: pore-bearing animals with a porous body and canal system - e.g. Sycon/sponge. Coelenterata (Cnidaria): aquatic animals with a hollow body cavity and stinging cells, radial symmetry - e.g. Hydra/jellyfish. Arthropoda: animals with jointed legs, a chitin exoskeleton and a segmented body; the largest phylum - e.g. insects/prawn.
questions.explanation: Feature plus example for each phylum.

questions.question: How do amphibians differ from reptiles?
questions.answer: Amphibians (e.g. frog, toad) have a moist skin, can live both in water and on land, and usually lay eggs in water; their young often pass through an aquatic larval stage. Reptiles (e.g. lizard, snake, turtle) have a dry, scaly skin, are fully adapted to life on land (they creep), and lay shelled eggs on land. Both are cold-blooded vertebrates.
questions.explanation: Skin, habitat and reproduction distinguish them.

questions.question: What are the defining characteristics of the phylum Chordata?
questions.answer: Chordates have, at some stage of life, a notochord (a flexible supporting rod), a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal gill slits. The advanced chordates (vertebrates) have the notochord replaced by a backbone (vertebral column).
questions.explanation: Notochord, dorsal nerve cord, gill slits.

questions.question: List three characteristic features of mammals.
questions.answer: (1) Their bodies are covered with hair. (2) Females possess mammary glands that produce milk to feed their young. (3) They are warm-blooded (maintain a constant body temperature) and most give birth to live young. Examples: human, dog, whale.

questions.question: Why is Kingdom Protista said to form a link between Monera and the higher kingdoms?
questions.answer: Protista consists of unicellular EUKARYOTES. They are more advanced than the prokaryotic Monera (because they possess a true nucleus and organelles), yet simpler than the multicellular Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Thus they bridge the gap between the simple prokaryotes and the complex multicellular kingdoms.
questions.explanation: Unicellular eukaryotes bridge prokaryotes and higher kingdoms.

questions.question: 'The five kingdom system is more natural than the two-kingdom system.' Justify this statement.
questions.answer: The two-kingdom system used only two broad groups (plants and animals) and ignored fundamental cell-level differences, so it lumped bacteria, fungi and protists with plants or animals. The five kingdom system instead uses cell structure (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body organisation and mode of nutrition, so it separates prokaryotes (Monera) from eukaryotes, places unicellular eukaryotes in Protista, and gives fungi their own kingdom. Because the groupings reflect real evolutionary and cellular relationships, the five kingdom system is considered more natural.
questions.explanation: Five kingdoms reflect cellular/evolutionary relationships more accurately.

questions.question: Why is a system of classification compared to arranging books on shelves in a library?
questions.answer: Just as a library with millions of books needs shelves and a catalogue so that any book can be found quickly, the millions of living organisms need to be arranged into orderly groups so that they can be studied, identified and located easily. Without classification, studying or finding information about any particular organism among such enormous diversity would be almost impossible.
questions.explanation: Classification brings order to vast diversity, like library shelving.

questions.question: A student examined four organisms in the laboratory: (i) a bacterium, which is a single cell with no true nucleus; (ii) Amoeba, a single cell with a true nucleus; (iii) a mushroom, which is multicellular, has chitin walls and feeds on dead matter; (iv) a money plant, which is green and makes its own food. Answer the following: (a) To which kingdom does the bacterium belong? (b) To which kingdom does Amoeba belong, and why? (c) Name the kingdom of the mushroom and its mode of nutrition. (d) State why the money plant is placed in Plantae.
questions.answer: (a) The bacterium belongs to Kingdom MONERA (it is prokaryotic - no true nucleus). (b) Amoeba belongs to Kingdom PROTISTA, because it is a unicellular organism with a true (eukaryotic) nucleus. (c) The mushroom belongs to Kingdom FUNGI; its mode of nutrition is heterotrophic and saprophytic (it absorbs nutrients from dead and decaying matter). (d) The money plant is placed in PLANTAE because it is multicellular, eukaryotic, has cellulose cell walls and is autotrophic (it contains chlorophyll and makes its own food by photosynthesis).
questions.explanation: Applies the defining features of Monera, Protista, Fungi and Plantae to classify each organism.

questions.question: Read the following and answer the questions. Carl Linnaeus introduced a system in which every organism is given a two-part Latin name. For example, the scientific name of the mango is Mangifera indica and that of human beings is Homo sapiens. (a) What is this naming system called? (b) In the name Mangifera indica, which part is the genus and which is the species? (c) State two rules for writing such a name. (d) Why are scientific names preferred over common names?
questions.answer: (a) The system is called BINOMIAL NOMENCLATURE. (b) In Mangifera indica, 'Mangifera' is the genus (generic name) and 'indica' is the species (specific name). (c) Rules: the name is written in Latin and italics (underlined separately when handwritten); the genus name begins with a capital letter while the species name begins with a small letter. (d) Scientific names are preferred because common names vary from place to place and language to language, causing confusion, whereas a scientific name is single and universally accepted, so scientists everywhere refer to the same organism by the same name.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of binomial nomenclature, its parts, rules and purpose.

questions.question: A gardener observed two plants. Plant A had leaves with parallel venation, a fibrous root system, and its seeds split into a single piece. Plant B had leaves with net-like (reticulate) venation, a tap root, and its seeds split into two pieces. Both produced flowers with seeds enclosed in fruits. (a) To which major plant group (with seeds enclosed in a fruit) do both plants belong? (b) Identify Plant A as a monocot or a dicot, giving a reason. (c) Identify Plant B, giving a reason. (d) Give one example of each type.
questions.answer: (a) Both plants are ANGIOSPERMS (flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed within a fruit). (b) Plant A is a MONOCOTYLEDON (monocot), because its seed has a single cotyledon, its leaves show parallel venation and it has a fibrous root system. (c) Plant B is a DICOTYLEDON (dicot), because its seed has two cotyledons, its leaves show reticulate venation and it has a tap root. (d) Example of a monocot: maize (or wheat, grass); example of a dicot: gram (or mango, rose).
questions.explanation: Applies monocot/dicot distinguishing features to identify each plant within the angiosperms.

questions.question: Four animals were studied: (i) a frog with moist skin that lives in water and on land; (ii) a lizard with dry scaly skin that creeps on land; (iii) a pigeon with feathers and wings; (iv) a dog with body hair that feeds its young on milk. All four have a backbone. (a) To which phylum do all four belong? (b) Name the class of the frog and the lizard. (c) Name the class of the pigeon and state one feature that places it there. (d) Name the class of the dog and give two features.
questions.answer: (a) All four are vertebrates and belong to the phylum CHORDATA. (b) The frog belongs to class AMPHIBIA (moist skin, lives in water and on land); the lizard belongs to class REPTILIA (dry, scaly skin, creeps on land). (c) The pigeon belongs to class AVES; a feature placing it there is the presence of feathers and wings (it is also warm-blooded with a beak). (d) The dog belongs to class MAMMALIA; two features: its body is covered with hair, and the female has mammary glands that produce milk to feed the young (it is also warm-blooded).
questions.explanation: Applies vertebrate-class features to classify amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals within Chordata.

questions.question: A teacher told her class: 'There are more than a million known species of living organisms, and biologists keep discovering new ones. Yet we are able to study them in an organised way.' She then asked the class to think about how this is possible. (a) What term describes the arrangement of organisms into groups based on similarities and differences? (b) Name the branch of biology that deals with this. (c) Give two advantages of doing this. (d) What would studying organisms be like without it?
questions.answer: (a) The term is CLASSIFICATION. (b) The branch of biology is TAXONOMY (systematics). (c) Two advantages: it makes the study of the huge variety of organisms simple and systematic (we study representative members of each group), and it reveals the relationships among groups and provides a common scientific language for identification. (d) Without classification, studying organisms would be chaotic and almost impossible - like searching a huge library with no shelves or catalogue - because each of the million-plus organisms would have to be dealt with separately.
questions.explanation: Tests the meaning, science and advantages of classification.

questions.question: Before 1969, all living things were divided into just two kingdoms - Plantae and Animalia. Bacteria were placed with plants, and so were fungi; Euglena puzzled biologists because it swims using a flagellum yet also carries out photosynthesis. (a) Name the two kingdoms of the old system. (b) Why was placing bacteria with plants a problem? (c) Why could Euglena not be placed satisfactorily? (d) Name the scientist whose new system solved these problems.
questions.answer: (a) The two kingdoms were PLANTAE and ANIMALIA. (b) Bacteria are PROKARYOTIC (no true nucleus), whereas plants are eukaryotic; lumping them together ignored this fundamental cell-level difference, so the system was not natural. (c) Euglena could not be placed satisfactorily because it shows BOTH animal-like features (it moves using a flagellum and can ingest food) and plant-like features (it photosynthesises), so it fits neither kingdom cleanly. (d) R. H. WHITTAKER, who proposed the five kingdom classification in 1969.
questions.explanation: Tests the limitations of the two-kingdom system and the move to five kingdoms.

questions.question: Whittaker classified organisms using three criteria. Consider: a bread mould (Rhizopus) growing on stale bread absorbs nutrients from it; a green alga (Spirogyra) in a pond makes its own food; a bacterium in soil has no nucleus. (a) State the three criteria Whittaker used. (b) Which kingdom does Rhizopus belong to and on which criterion? (c) Why is the bacterium NOT placed in the same kingdom as Spirogyra? (d) Which kingdom is the green alga placed in?
questions.answer: (a) Whittaker's three criteria were: cell structure (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular/multicellular), and mode of nutrition (autotrophic/heterotrophic). (b) Rhizopus belongs to Kingdom FUNGI, mainly on the criterion of nutrition - it is heterotrophic/saprophytic, absorbing food from dead matter, and has chitin walls. (c) The bacterium is PROKARYOTIC (no true nucleus) so it is placed in Monera, whereas Spirogyra is a eukaryote; the difference in cell structure separates them. (d) The green alga Spirogyra is placed in Kingdom PLANTAE (it is autotrophic with cellulose walls; in some schemes simple algae are treated under Thallophyta of Plantae).
questions.explanation: Applies Whittaker's three criteria to distinguish kingdoms.

questions.question: The classification of a domestic cat is given partly as: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae, Genus Felis, Species domestica. (a) Arrange these categories from the largest to the smallest. (b) Which category is the basic unit of classification? (c) As we move from Kingdom to Species, what happens to the number of shared characteristics? (d) Write the scientific name of the cat.
questions.answer: (a) Largest to smallest: Kingdom (Animalia) > Phylum (Chordata) > Class (Mammalia) > Order (Carnivora) > Family (Felidae) > Genus (Felis) > Species (domestica). (b) The SPECIES is the basic unit of classification. (c) As we move from Kingdom down to Species, the number of shared characteristics INCREASES (organisms become more closely related), while the number of organisms in each group decreases. (d) The scientific name of the cat is Felis domestica (genus capitalised, species in small letters, written in italics).
questions.explanation: Tests the taxonomic hierarchy, the basic unit, the trend in shared characters, and binomial naming.

questions.question: On a nature walk, students saw: (i) Spirogyra, a slimy green thread in a pond with no roots, stems or leaves; (ii) a moss on a damp wall; (iii) a fern with proper roots, stems and leaves but no flowers or seeds; (iv) a pine tree bearing cones with naked seeds. (a) Name the plant group of Spirogyra. (b) Why are mosses called 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'? (c) Why is the fern placed in Pteridophyta and not in the seed plants? (d) Name the plant group of the pine tree.
questions.answer: (a) Spirogyra belongs to THALLOPHYTA (algae) - it has no true roots, stems or leaves; its body is a thallus. (b) Mosses (Bryophyta) are called 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' because, although they live on land, they NEED WATER for reproduction (fertilisation), so they depend on both land and water. (c) The fern is placed in PTERIDOPHYTA because it has true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue but bears NO SEEDS (it reproduces by spores), so it cannot be grouped with the seed-bearing plants. (d) The pine tree is a GYMNOSPERM (it bears naked seeds in cones).
questions.explanation: Applies features of the major plant groups to identify each specimen.

questions.question: A student wrote four scientific names in his notebook: 'homo sapiens', 'Mangifera Indica', 'Rana tigrina' and 'PISUM SATIVUM'. His teacher said only one was written correctly. (a) Which name is written correctly? (b) Correct the name of the human being. (c) What is wrong with the way the mango's name is written? (d) State the rule about capital and small letters in a scientific name.
questions.answer: (a) Only 'Rana tigrina' is written correctly (genus capitalised, species in small letters). (b) The human being's name should be written as Homo sapiens (capital H for the genus, small s for the species). (c) In 'Mangifera Indica' the species name 'Indica' is wrongly capitalised; it should be written as Mangifera indica with a small 'i'. (d) The rule is: the GENUS name begins with a CAPITAL letter while the SPECIES name begins with a SMALL (lowercase) letter; the whole name is written in italics (or underlined separately when handwritten).
questions.explanation: Applies the rules of binomial nomenclature to correct wrongly written names.
